ig_carousel_topic.topic: The Kelly criterion — explained without the math degree
ig_carousel_topic.slide1_text:
How much should you actually bet?
Most bettors guess. Kelly gives you a framework.
ig_carousel_topic.slide2_text:
The common mistake: flat-betting every play the same size regardless of edge or odds.

A +102 play with a real 55% win probability is not the same bet as a -136 play with a 52% edge. Treating them identically leaks money over time.
ig_carousel_topic.slide3_text:
Kelly's core idea: bet a fraction of your bankroll proportional to your edge.

Bigger edge + better odds = larger bet. Smaller edge = smaller bet. No edge = no bet.

The formula exists, but the concept is what changes how you think.
ig_carousel_topic.slide4_text:
Simple example:
You have a 55% win probability on a +102 line.
Full Kelly says bet about 7.9% of your bankroll.
Most serious bettors use Half Kelly (≈4%) to cushion against model error.

On a $1,000 roll, that's a $40 bet — not $200.
ig_carousel_topic.slide5_text:
Kelly won't make you win more often.
It helps you not blow up when variance hits — and it will hit.

Size your bets like your bankroll matters. Because it does.
